repositories_and_sources.research_scope: Primary repositories, official dataset pages, and linked papers for multi-component food detection, ingredient recognition, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, panoptic segmentation, and the mass-ground-truth sources needed to turn masks into nutrition estimates.

entries.name: FoodSeg103 and FoodSeg154
entries.role: Fine-grained semantic food and ingredient segmentation benchmark with official MMsegmentation-style baselines and ReLeM checkpoints.
entries.production_starting_point: Useful as an academic semantic-segmentation benchmark and teacher-data source; not sufficient by itself for production because it has no mass labels, no instance identity, and the dataset download terms are not clearly stated.
entries.primary_evidence: The repository README documents 7,118 images, 104 label IDs in the repository convention, an average of about six ingredient labels per image, pixel-wise masks, Apache-2.0 code, and baseline mIoU values. The paper and project page document the 9,490-image FoodSeg103 plus FoodSeg154 release with 154 ingredient classes.

entries.name: FoodInsSeg
entries.role: Ingredient-level food instance-segmentation dataset and COCO-format evaluation/visualization code.
entries.production_starting_point: Strongest public benchmark for ingredient-level instance masks, but not legally usable as-is in a commercial product because the dataset is explicitly academic/non-commercial under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
entries.primary_evidence: The official repository reports 7,118 images, 103 categories, 119,048 ingredient-level masks, polygon annotations, and an InsSAM-tool origin for the instance labels.

entries.name: FoodSAM
entries.role: A research pipeline combining SAM, a semantic segmenter, and an object detector to produce semantic, instance, panoptic, and promptable food segmentation.
entries.production_starting_point: Useful for server-side experiments, teacher-mask generation, and comparing task formulations; a poor direct mobile starting point because it chains several GPU-oriented models and depends on restricted research datasets/checkpoints.
entries.primary_evidence: The official README documents semantic and panoptic inference commands, an instance-segmentation path, FoodSeg103 and UECFoodPixComplete evaluation, and FoodSAM mIoU of 46.42 on FoodSeg103 and 66.14 on UECFoodPixComplete.

entries.name: MyFoodRepo-273 and Food Recognition Benchmark
entries.role: Real-world user-photo benchmark with individual food-item polygons, class labels, and Detectron2/MMDetection starter code; the benchmark also discusses weight/volume tasks.
entries.production_starting_point: Best public-domain candidate for testing wild phone-photo robustness and multi-item detection, subject to a separate data-rights/privacy/commercial-use review; the released polygons do not establish per-component gram ground truth.
entries.primary_evidence: The paper reports 24,119 images, 39,325 polygons, 273 classes, and private test rounds of about 5,000 images. The GitHub starter kit provides MIT-licensed baseline code for mmdetection and detectron2.

entries.name: UECFoodPixComplete
entries.role: Large semantic food segmentation dataset derived from UECFood-100, with manually refined pixel masks and category IDs.
entries.production_starting_point: Useful for semantic segmentation pretraining and Japanese/Asian food-domain evaluation; not directly usable for a commercial product because the official page restricts use to non-commercial research.
entries.primary_evidence: The official page documents 9,000 training and 1,000 test images, 103 category labels in its label table, 759 MB for UECFoodPixComplete, and manual mask refinement over the earlier GrabCut version.

entries.name: UNIMIB2016 and Semantic Food Detection
entries.role: Canteen-tray semantic food detection/segmentation benchmark with polygon boundaries, bounding boxes, and labels for individual food items.
entries.production_starting_point: Useful as a small multi-component tray benchmark and European-canteen domain slice; too small and too institution-specific to be the sole production training source.
entries.primary_evidence: The dataset paper reports 1,027 tray images, 73 food categories, and 3,616 food instances captured with a Samsung Galaxy S3 in a semi-controlled canteen environment.

entries.name: Food Instance Segmentation using Synthetic Data
entries.role: Blender-generated multi-object meal scenes, Mask R-CNN training/evaluation/inference code, and released weights for food instance segmentation.
entries.production_starting_point: Useful for synthetic pretraining, augmentation, and testing a mask pipeline before real-data fine-tuning; not a substitute for consented real phone photos and its repository does not state a clear commercial data/model license.
entries.primary_evidence: The paper reports a real-world mask AP@all of 52.2% from synthetic-only training and a 6.4 percentage-point improvement after fine-tuning; the repository documents Blender data and Mask R-CNN code.

entries.name: Nutrition5k
entries.role: Paired visual-nutrition dataset supplying ingredient lists, per-ingredient grams, total mass, calories, macronutrients, multi-view RGB video, and overhead RGB-D; it is not itself an ingredient-mask dataset.
entries.production_starting_point: Best public source for building and validating a mass/portion head and for designing weighed capture; not a complete visible-ingredient segmentation starter because per-ingredient pixel masks/bounding boxes are not provided.
entries.primary_evidence: The official repository reports 5,006 plates, four rotating side-angle videos per plate, overhead RGB-D when available, per-ingredient mass, official splits, regression scripts, a 181.4 GB download, and a California cafeteria bias disclaimer.

entries.name: BenchSeg
entries.role: Emerging multi-view food-video segmentation and temporal-consistency benchmark with segmenter plus memory-tracking baselines.
entries.production_starting_point: Useful for evaluating camera-motion robustness, mask flicker, temporal continuity, and multi-view capture; not a first mobile model because the repository requires Docker/submodules and large checkpoints, and its public pages do not document a commercial license or a unified ingredient taxonomy.
entries.primary_evidence: The paper and project page report 55 dish scenes aggregated from Nutrition5k, Vegetables & Fruits, MetaFood3D, and FoodKit, with 25,284 annotated frames and free 360-degree camera motion.

entries.name: Food Ingredients Recognition through Multi-label Learning and Dishscan
entries.role: Image-level multi-label ingredient detection rather than localization; Ingredients101 and Recipes5k provide recipe/ingredient supervision, while Dishscan evaluates encoders including MobileNet.
entries.production_starting_point: Useful as a low-cost candidate-generator baseline for ingredient presence, but not an ingredient-boundary or portion model; the older Keras/Theano-style code needs substantial modernization and its data rights must be checked separately.
entries.primary_evidence: The official repository documents Ingredients101 with 446 unique ingredients across 101 Food101 types and Recipes5k with 4,826 recipes, 3,213 fine-grained ingredients, and a 1,013-ingredient simplified vocabulary.

maintenance_and_reproducibility.status_summary: [uncertain] This is a snapshot as of 2026-07-31; GitHub stars, issue counts, commit activity, download links, checkpoints, and dataset terms can change. The landscape is research-maintained rather than production-maintained: most repos have no releases, no mobile artifact, no CI evidence for deployment, and GPU-centric setup instructions.

observations.reproducibility_risk: The paper describes FoodSeg154/9,490 images while the repository README is centered on FoodSeg103/7,118 images; pin the dataset variant, class map, checkpoint, and split before training.

observations.observed_maintenance: 11 commits, 0 issues, 0 releases, a small evaluation/visualization codebase, and dataset downloads via Google Drive or Baidu Netdisk.
observations.reproducibility_risk: The COCO format is clear, but access is manual, there is no maintained training pipeline or mobile conversion, and the dataset agreement can terminate access.

observations.observed_maintenance: 58 commits, 13 issues, 1 pull request, 182 stars, Apache-2.0 model/repository statement, and working command examples for semantic/panoptic inference.
observations.reproducibility_risk: Installation spans SAM, MMsegmentation, UniDet, CUDA, and multiple checkpoints; open issues include checkpoint/setup failures. Treat it as a reproducible research baseline only after freezing dependency versions and verifying every checkpoint hash.

observations.observed_maintenance: The GitHub starter kit has 121 commits and MIT code; the linked GitLab experiment project has 32 commits, one branch, zero tags, and Apache-2.0 metadata.
observations.reproducibility_risk: The public training data and older challenge rounds are usable for benchmark reproduction, but private test data, challenge endpoints, participant artifacts, and data-use terms are external to the GitHub checkout.

observations.observed_maintenance: Both are stable academic datasets with direct institutional pages and simple image/mask or polygon formats, but neither has a modern maintained mobile training repository.
observations.reproducibility_risk: Older download pages, HTTP links, class-index conventions, and missing explicit version hashes make it necessary to archive the downloaded data, checksums, label map, and license text internally.

observations.observed_maintenance: 14 commits, 1 issue, 0 releases visible on the repository page; training, inference, evaluation, Blender dataset, and pretrained-weight links are present.
observations.reproducibility_risk: The repository does not document a stable dataset version, exact Blender scene generation seed, or model/data license. Reproduce only inside an isolated environment and treat the released weights as research inputs.

observations.observed_maintenance: The official GitHub repository was archived by its owner on 2026-04-19 and is read-only; it has 11 commits, official splits, shell/data scripts, 412 stars, and a very large 181.4 GB download.
observations.reproducibility_risk: The content is unusually well documented, but storage and transfer costs are material and the dataset's cafeteria/capture bias is not solved by its large size.

observations.observed_maintenance: 42 commits, a dev branch, 0 stars, 0 issues, Docker/submodule setup, 8.15 GB of pretrained models, and explicit inference/evaluation scripts.
observations.reproducibility_risk: It is a very recent research release; pin the dev commit, external SAM2/XMem2 revisions, model URLs, source-dataset permissions, and annotation release before relying on it.

observations.source: Dishscan and the older multi-label repository
observations.observed_maintenance: Dishscan has 12 commits, 0 releases, and MIT code; the older reference implementation has 23 commits and no visible release. Both are baseline research code, not maintained production SDKs.
observations.reproducibility_risk: Environment files and legacy Keras dependencies are likely to require repair; the repos do not provide a complete mobile inference contract, calibration, monitoring, or rollback path.

reproducibility_requirements_for_supernu: Freeze a repository commit, dataset archive checksum, class-index map, split files, pretrained checkpoint checksum, preprocessing dimensions, and evaluation script version.
Keep repository code, dataset rights, model/checkpoint rights, and downstream nutrition-catalog rights as separate approvals.

Re-run benchmark evaluation on a held-out, person/recipe/device/time-separated SuperNutrition corpus; published scores on FoodSeg103, UECFoodPixComplete, or Nutrition5k are not phone-photo acceptance evidence.

license_and_usage.commercial_readiness_summary: [uncertain] Code licenses are often permissive while the image/mask dataset terms are academic-only, unspecified, or inherited from third parties. No repository in this landscape should be copied into a commercial mobile product until code, weights, images, annotations, and derived-model rights are reviewed separately.

Academic-only segmentation datasets can still be used to design labels, test algorithms internally where permitted, or generate research comparisons, but not silently converted into a shipped model.

landscape_matrix.labels: Food/ingredient categories; FoodSeg103 repository convention exposes 103 foreground categories plus background-like label IDs, while the paper's extension reports 154 ingredient classes.
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Pixel-wise semantic mask with one category per pixel; multiple ingredients can appear in one image, but separate touching instances of the same ingredient are not distinguished.
landscape_matrix.detection_or_instance: No official object-detection or instance-ID annotation in the core benchmark.
landscape_matrix.panoptic: No official panoptic ground truth; FoodSAM can derive panoptic predictions from it.

landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: COCO-style polygons with one annotation per food item/ingredient instance, category ID, area, and bounding box; repeated items can have distinct instances.
landscape_matrix.detection_or_instance: Directly supports instance masks and boxes; COCO evaluation code is supplied.
landscape_matrix.panoptic: No official panoptic category/thing-stuff ground truth is advertised.

landscape_matrix.labels: Semantic food categories from FoodSeg103/UECFoodPixComplete plus detector-provided non-food/background categories.
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Composed output: coarse semantic class masks are refined or split with SAM masks; detector prompts provide non-food objects for panoptic composition.
landscape_matrix.detection_or_instance: Uses a detector and SAM-generated masks; not a single compact end-to-end ingredient detector.
landscape_matrix.panoptic: Explicitly supported by the official paper and repository.

landscape_matrix.labels: 273 food classes selected with at least 35 annotations per class in the benchmark release.
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Human-verified polygons for individual visible food items; usually one to two items per image, with a long tail up to 12 polygons in an image.
landscape_matrix.detection_or_instance: Directly supports object/instance prediction in COCO-like benchmark workflows.
landscape_matrix.panoptic: No panoptic stuff labels or ingredient-level hidden-recipe labels.

landscape_matrix.labels: Official label table provides food category IDs; the page describes 103 class labels, while some papers index the foreground/background set as 102/103 categories. [uncertain]
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Pixel-wise semantic masks manually refined from GrabCut masks; all pixels of a category share a class value, with no instance IDs.
landscape_matrix.detection_or_instance: No instance-level identity in the official format.

landscape_matrix.labels: 73 food categories and individual food identities.
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Per-item polygon boundary, bounding box, and food label on a tray image.
landscape_matrix.detection_or_instance: Supports individual visible-item localization, although it predates modern COCO instance conventions.

tasks: object detection through Mask R-CNN outputs
landscape_matrix.labels: Synthetic food-object categories defined by the Blender scenes/model configuration rather than a shared ingredient ontology.
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Instance masks, boxes, and class IDs generated from 3D scenes; real-world evaluation tests transfer to food items.

landscape_matrix.labels: Fine-grained ingredient IDs and names in metadata, with per-ingredient grams and nutrient values.
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Dish-level visual frames plus structured ingredient metadata; the official dataset does not provide per-ingredient pixel masks or boxes.
landscape_matrix.detection_or_instance: No direct component detector/instance mask ground truth in the dataset.

landscape_matrix.labels: Food segmentation labels and scene/frame identities; a single unified ingredient taxonomy is not documented on the public abstract/project page.
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Per-frame masks with temporal continuity evaluation; the benchmark adds continuity, flicker-rate, and IoU-drift metrics.
landscape_matrix.detection_or_instance: Supports segmenter and memory-tracker comparisons, not clearly a COCO ingredient-instance benchmark.

landscape_matrix.labels: Ingredients101: 446 unique ingredients across 101 Food101 food types; Recipes5k: 3,213 fine-grained or 1,013 simplified ingredients across 4,826 recipes.
landscape_matrix.annotation_granularity: Image-level list of ingredients, including ingredients that may be visually hidden inside a recipe; no pixel localization.

task_and_labels.key_labeling_distinction: The word ingredient is used at different levels: a visible food component in FoodSeg103/FoodInsSeg, a visible food item in MyFoodRepo/UNIMIB, and a recipe constituent that may be invisible in Ingredients101/Recipes5k/Nutrition5k. These labels are not interchangeable without an explicit ontology and visible-versus-hidden flag.

dataset_matrix.scale: FoodSeg103 repository: 7,118 images; paper extension: 9,490 images across FoodSeg103 and FoodSeg154.
dataset_matrix.splits: The repository provides benchmark train/test organization; the exact variant and split files must be pinned because the paper's extension and README emphasize different counts.
dataset_matrix.domain: Web-collected food images with multiple visible ingredients and substantial overlap/appearance variation; broad but not a controlled phone-photo cohort.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: Average about six ingredient labels per image according to the official project/paper.

dataset_matrix.scale: 7,118 images, 119,048 masks; 4,983 train images/82,716 masks and 2,135 test images/36,332 masks.
dataset_matrix.splits: Same train/test split as FoodSeg103; average 16.59 masks per train image and 17.01 per test image; maximum 126 train masks and 186 test masks in one image.
dataset_matrix.domain: FoodSeg103-derived images, so it increases annotation granularity more than capture diversity.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: High instance count per image makes it valuable for crowded mixed meals, but it inherits the source dataset's taxonomy and web-image bias.

dataset_matrix.scale: No separate new image corpus; reported experiments use FoodSeg103 and UECFoodPixComplete.
dataset_matrix.splits: Uses the underlying benchmark splits and checkpoint-specific evaluation scripts.
dataset_matrix.domain: Mixed food images plus non-food background objects; zero-shot/promptable behavior is research-oriented.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: Useful for testing multiple outputs from one image, not for expanding the domain distribution.

dataset_matrix.scale: 24,119 public training images and 39,325 polygons across 273 classes; round test sets contain about 5,000 private images.
dataset_matrix.splits: train-v0.4 is public; challenge test sets are private and round-specific.
dataset_matrix.domain: Real user photos from the MyFoodRepo app, including free-living meal images rather than only curated web images; source population is strongly connected to Swiss nutrition cohorts.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: 15,701 images have one polygon, 4,397 have two, 2,341 have three, then a long tail to 12 polygons; this is realistic for detection but less dense than FoodInsSeg.

dataset_matrix.scale: 10,000 images total: 9,000 train and 1,000 test; 103-category label table in the official page.
dataset_matrix.splits: Official train.txt and test.txt lists are provided in the archive.
dataset_matrix.domain: UECFood-100-derived Japanese and mixed food photos with multiple foods on plates, varied camera angles, arrangements, and touching regions.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: Strong semantic multi-food benchmark; it has no per-component mass or instance identity.

dataset_matrix.scale: 1,027 tray images, 73 food categories, and 3,616 annotated food instances; common experimental split is about 650 train and 360 test images.
dataset_matrix.splits: The published paper and subsequent experiments use fixed research splits; preserve the official annotations and do not mix near-duplicate trays across splits.
dataset_matrix.domain: Semi-controlled Italian university canteen trays captured with a Samsung Galaxy S3, including plates, placemats, multiple foods, and sides served together.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: Good for crowded tray layout and European canteen evaluation, weak for global cuisine diversity and modern smartphone capture.

dataset_matrix.scale: Blender-generated data and a real-world evaluation set are released through external links; the primary README does not state a stable image-count summary.
dataset_matrix.splits: Repository configs define training/evaluation paths, but a versioned public split manifest is not prominent.
dataset_matrix.domain: Synthetic plate scenes with controllable object placement, lighting, and masks; real-world transfer is the stated evaluation target.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: Supports controlled multi-object occlusion and synthetic rare cases, but the sim-to-real gap is substantial.

dataset_matrix.scale: 5,006 plates with four rotating side-angle videos, overhead RGB-D when available, fine-grained ingredients, and per-ingredient mass.
dataset_matrix.splits: Official dish-ID train/test split keeps all incremental scans from a unique plate in one split.
dataset_matrix.domain: A few Google cafeterias in California, captured with a custom scanning rig; approximately 181.4 GB for the complete archive.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: Ingredients are added incrementally, growing from simple items to complex mixed plates; excellent paired nutrition detail but narrow cuisine/capture diversity.

dataset_matrix.scale: 55 dish scenes and 25,284 annotated frames, including source scenes from Nutrition5k, Vegetables & Fruits, MetaFood3D, and FoodKit.
dataset_matrix.splits: Project scripts define benchmark evaluation; pin the dev branch and the external source-dataset versions.
dataset_matrix.domain: Free 360-degree camera motion and multi-view food video, closer to viewpoint-robust capture research than a single still phone photo.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: Best fit for temporal/multi-view stability and mask tracking; it is not a broad recipe/ingredient corpus.

dataset_matrix.scale: Ingredients101 covers 101 Food101 types and 446 unique ingredients; Recipes5k contains 4,826 recipes, 3,213 fine-grained ingredients, or 1,013 simplified ingredients.
dataset_matrix.splits: The reference repo documents balanced train/validation/test splits by food type and recipe alternatives.
dataset_matrix.domain: Food101-derived web images and recipe metadata, with strong recipe/composition supervision but no real-world mask or portion protocol.
dataset_matrix.meal_composition: Useful for multi-label candidate generation and hidden-recipe ingredient reasoning, not visible component geometry.

dataset_scale_and_domain.domain_gap_summary: No single public source combines broad cuisines, real phone photos, ingredient-level instance masks, panoptic non-food context, and independently weighed per-component grams. The landscape is inherently compositional: segmentation sources provide geometry, multi-label sources provide recipe constituents, and Nutrition5k provides controlled mass/nutrition labels.

expected_ingredient_quality.quality_summary: [uncertain] Expected transfer to SuperNutrition is uncertain because published benchmarks use different taxonomies, image sources, capture rigs, and split protocols. The most reliable product behavior should be visible-component candidate generation with abstention and user correction, not hidden-ingredient certainty.

evidence_by_source.published_signal: Repository baselines report mIoU from 27.8 to 35.5 depending architecture, and ReLeM-R50/FPN reports 29.1 in the README table; the paper establishes the benchmark as difficult because ingredients overlap and one ingredient changes appearance across dishes.
evidence_by_source.likely_strength: Visible, sufficiently large components with a known 103/154-class vocabulary.
evidence_by_source.likely_failure: Touching/overlapping ingredients, sauces, mixed recipes, rare cuisines, and same-class instance separation.

evidence_by_source.published_signal: 119,048 instance masks with up to 186 masks in one test image provide much denser supervision than semantic-only datasets; the official repo supplies COCO evaluation but does not publish a single headline mask-AP score.
evidence_by_source.likely_strength: Separating repeated visible components and training a compact instance segmenter.
evidence_by_source.likely_failure: Inherited FoodSeg103 appearance/domain bias, small or heavily occluded ingredients, and any hidden ingredient not visibly present.

evidence_by_source.published_signal: FoodSAM reports 46.42 mIoU on FoodSeg103 and 66.14 mIoU on UECFoodPixComplete, and supports semantic, instance, panoptic, and promptable outputs.
evidence_by_source.likely_strength: Flexible mask proposals, interactive correction, and non-food/background separation in research settings.
evidence_by_source.likely_failure: Heavy multi-model composition, category errors inherited from the semantic/detector stages, mask over/under-segmentation, and poor mobile cost.

evidence_by_source.published_signal: Benchmark leaders reached mAP 0.568 in round 4 and mean average recall 0.885 in round 3 on private same-platform test sets.
evidence_by_source.likely_strength: Real-world user-photo object detection and visible food-item localization.
evidence_by_source.likely_failure: Class imbalance, out-of-taxonomy foods, clutter, cultural/cuisine shift, merged dishes, and no direct evidence that polygons translate to ingredient-level or gram-level accuracy.

evidence_by_source.published_signal: UECFoodPixComplete's official DeepLabV3+ experiment reports 0.555 mIoU; UNIMIB2016 provides fine polygons on multi-food trays and is useful for spatial evaluation.
evidence_by_source.likely_strength: Large visible regions and tray/plate food-background separation.
evidence_by_source.likely_failure: Semantic masks merge same-class instances, food-specific regional bias, placemat/plate background confusion, and no hidden-recipe or quantity signal.

evidence_by_source.published_signal: Synthetic-only training achieved 52.2% mask AP@all on a real-world set, with a further 6.4 percentage-point improvement after real-data fine-tuning.
evidence_by_source.likely_strength: Controlled geometry, occlusion, lighting, and rare composition augmentation.
evidence_by_source.likely_failure: Texture, cooking state, sauces, deformable food, restaurant presentation, and camera-domain shift.

evidence_by_source.published_signal: The benchmark reports that ordinary image segmenters degrade under novel viewpoints while memory-augmented methods improve temporal consistency, measured with continuity, flicker rate, and IoU drift.
evidence_by_source.likely_strength: Stable masks across short video/multi-view capture and detection of temporal failure modes invisible to single-frame mIoU.
evidence_by_source.likely_failure: Still-image phone workflows, rapid motion/blur, ingredient identity, and transfer from research cameras/source datasets.

production_metrics: Visible-component recall and missed-component rate, including a separate score for small/occluded/sauce components.
Per-class macro-F1, top-1/top-5 candidate recall, calibration error, abstention/selective-risk curves, and correction acceptance/time.
Semantic class-balanced mIoU and pixel accuracy; instance mask AP/mAR across IoU thresholds; panoptic PQ/SQ/RQ only if panoptic labels are collected.
Per-cuisine, device, lighting, camera-angle, raw/cooked-state, mixed-dish, and component-size slices; no aggregate-only launch claim.
For video or guided multi-view capture, temporal continuity, flicker rate, IoU drift, and track identity switches.
expected_ingredient_quality.quality_conclusion: These datasets can make visible food decomposition materially better, but no published result establishes complete ingredient discovery, hidden-ingredient recall, allergen safety, or exact grams from one ordinary RGB photo.

source_matrix.source: FoodSeg103/FoodSeg154, FoodInsSeg, FoodSAM, UECFoodPixComplete, UNIMIB2016, BenchSeg
source_matrix.ground_truth: No grams, calibrated scale readings, per-component volume, or per-component depth-derived mass labels in the core sources.
source_matrix.implication: These sources can supervise where visible food is and what category it resembles, but not how much it weighs.

source_matrix.ground_truth: Public benchmark evidence establishes polygons and food classes; the starter kit mentions segmentation, classification, and weight/volume estimation as benchmark tasks, but the released 24,119-image dataset is not documented here as having verified per-polygon grams.
source_matrix.collection_method: User-submitted app photos with human polygon annotation; a public component-weighing protocol is not established.
source_matrix.implication: Use for visible-item detection/segmentation and domain testing, not as verified mass ground truth.

source_matrix.ground_truth: Per-ingredient grams, total dish mass, calories, fat, protein, and carbohydrate values.
source_matrix.collection_method: A custom sensor array and digital scale measured incremental weight as individual ingredients or prepared recipe items were added to each plate; nutrition values were derived from per-gram ingredient data and USDA Food and Nutrient Database mappings. Overhead RGB-D and four side-angle videos were captured for each scan when available.
source_matrix.implication: The strongest source for mass-regression supervision, but it does not align each gram label to a 2D ingredient mask and uses a cafeteria capture rig.

source_matrix.ground_truth: Ingredient presence/list labels and recipe composition; no independent mass scale ground truth in the code repository.
source_matrix.collection_method: Food type/recipe metadata and image-level ingredient lists.
source_matrix.implication: Useful for candidate generation and hidden-recipe research, not for portion calibration.

weight_ground_truth.bottom_line: The public landscape has a missing paired-corpus cell: phone-photo visible ingredient masks plus independently weighed per-component grams. SuperNutrition should collect that pairing rather than infer grams from mask area alone.

methods_by_source.input_and_output: RGB image to semantic pixels or per-item polygons/boxes/class IDs.
methods_by_source.geometry_assumption: None that identifies height, density, or mass; mask area is only a 2D visible-footprint proxy.
methods_by_source.reported_metrics: mIoU, pixel accuracy, mask AP/mAR, mAP, and mAR depending dataset.
methods_by_source.portion_readiness: Not weight-ready without a calibrated scale, depth/volume model, or user-entered serving reference.

methods_by_source.input_and_output: Phone/user image to food-item polygons/classes and benchmark predictions.
methods_by_source.geometry_assumption: No public evidence that the released polygon area is converted into grams; any weight/volume track must be verified from the specific challenge release.
methods_by_source.reported_metrics: Round 4 mAP 0.568 and round 3 mean average recall 0.885 for detection/segmentation benchmark results.
methods_by_source.portion_readiness: Good detection starting point, not a validated mass estimator.

methods_by_source.input_and_output: Overhead RGB, optional depth/volume scalar, and multi-view video to mass, calories, and macronutrient regression.
methods_by_source.geometry_assumption: Image-only mass regression, RGB-D/depth-as-fourth-channel, and explicit volume-assisted regression; the rig provides metric depth and scale-calibrated mass labels.
methods_by_source.reported_metrics: Original paper: RGB-only direct calorie MAE 26.1% and direct mass MAE 18.8%; RGB-D direct calorie MAE 18.8%; volume-assisted total mass MAE 13.7% (29.4 g); combined portion-independent plus volume-assisted end-to-end calorie MAE 16.5% (41.3 kcal).
methods_by_source.portion_readiness: Best benchmark for the mass head, but reported errors are under controlled cafeteria capture and should not be presented as ordinary phone-photo guarantees.

methods_by_source.input_and_output: Normalized phone RGB photo, optional device depth when available, visible-component masks, candidate identity, user-confirmed serving/portion input, and only then a catalog-grounded gram estimate.
methods_by_source.geometry_assumption: Use depth/scale only when device and calibration evidence supports it; otherwise treat grams as a broad estimate or require user correction instead of false precision.
methods_by_source.reported_metrics: Track grams MAE, signed bias, median absolute error, p90 absolute error, percentage within +/-20%, calibration/abstention, and separate errors for mixed dishes, sauces, occlusion, cuisines, devices, and raw/cooked states.
methods_by_source.portion_readiness: Production-ready only after a consented weighed validation set closes the G-3/G-5 acceptance gates.

portion_method_and_metrics.important_metric_warning: The 9.5% Nutrition5k calorie result is a portion-independent condition that relies on reliable mass information; it is not evidence that a single RGB phone image yields 9.5% calorie error.

identifiability_limits: A 2D mask measures visible footprint, not food height, density, compactness, water content, oil, or hidden layers.
The same visible area can correspond to different masses for leafy food, rice, meat, bread, sauces, or mixed recipes.
Occlusion and overlap cause both missed ingredients and double-counted regions; a semantic mask can merge adjacent same-class items.
Recipe ingredients such as oil, salt, flour, fillings, and blended components may be visually absent even when nutritionally important.
Depth improves geometry only when the sensor sees the surface, depth is calibrated, and the food shape/scale relationship is valid; device depth is not equivalent to a scale.
Nutrition5k's metric capture rig, California cafeteria menu, and incremental plating protocol do not represent all cuisines, home plates, restaurant photos, or ordinary phone angles.
false_precision_risks: Do not convert pixel area directly to grams or show exact gram values without a measured uncertainty model.
Do not infer hidden ingredients, allergen absence, or medical-safe nutrition from a segmentation mask.
Do not treat a high mIoU or mask AP as a calorie/portion metric; component identity and quantity are separate contracts.
Do not report a single average error when failure slices for sauces, occlusion, mixed dishes, cuisines, and small components are materially worse.
minimum_calibration_requirements: Metric or reference scale/depth when geometry is used.
Independent per-component and total mass measurement using a calibrated scale, with recipe/brand and raw/cooked state.
Uncertainty and abstention thresholds calibrated on held-out meals, not tuned on the product pilot test set.
User-visible correction for serving or portion and an explicit distinction between model estimate and catalog-derived nutrient calculation.

mobile_runtime_path.current_repository_reality: The primary repositories are Python/PyTorch/MMsegmentation/Detectron2/Mask R-CNN research code; FoodSAM and BenchSeg are multi-model or Docker/GPU pipelines, and none provides a supported Android/iOS production artifact for the complete ingredient-plus-weight task.

recommended_runtime_path.implementation: Use FoodSAM or a conventional Mask R-CNN/YOLO-seg/DeepLab baseline to compare semantic versus instance outputs on FoodSeg103, FoodInsSeg, UECFoodPixComplete, MyFoodRepo, and a newly collected corpus.
recommended_runtime_path.reason: Server GPUs make error analysis and annotation-tool integration easier before optimizing model size.

recommended_runtime_path.implementation: Train a compact detector/instance segmenter or semantic segmenter on cleared data, with a separate lightweight per-instance classifier/retriever. Export to ONNX Runtime Mobile, LiteRT, Core ML, or ExecuTorch after accuracy is frozen; use INT8/FP16 only after per-class and mask-quality checks.
recommended_runtime_path.reason: A single compact visible-component model is more realistic on Android/iOS than the FoodSAM three-model stack.

recommended_runtime_path.implementation: Keep RGB-only as the broad compatibility path. Add platform depth/AR/scale cues behind a separate port, with device capability reporting and calibration; do not make depth a silent prerequisite.
recommended_runtime_path.reason: Nutrition5k shows depth/volume can reduce mass error, but depth availability and quality vary by phone.

recommended_runtime_path.implementation: If local confidence is low or the meal is compositionally complex, offer a separately consented first-party remote route; preserve model/config version, provenance, deletion, and user correction in the shared inference contract.
recommended_runtime_path.reason: The architecture must not hide a photo upload or treat a cloud VLM's guessed ingredients/grams as nutrition authority.

mobile_constraints: Benchmark model file size, peak RAM, initialization time, p50/p95 latency, battery/thermal impact, and CPU/GPU/NPU fallback on named physical Android and iOS devices.
Keep image preprocessing, EXIF stripping, model version/checksum, and output schema deterministic across platforms.
Use segmentation masks for candidate review and serving guidance; compute displayed nutrients only after canonical catalog mapping and explicit serving confirmation.
Treat FoodSAM, BenchSeg, and full RGB-D Nutrition5k pipelines as research/server references rather than directly embedding them in the mobile app.

recommended_scale.pilot: 300-500 complete meals for protocol and model-selection work, with at least 100 genuinely multi-component meals and deliberate coverage of sauces, mixed dishes, occlusion, raw/cooked states, and culturally diverse foods.
recommended_scale.development: 1,500-3,000 meals for fine-tuning and slice analysis across devices, cuisines, homes/restaurants, lighting, camera angles, and repeated component classes.
recommended_scale.pre_release: 5,000 or more meals, or a statistically justified equivalent, with an untouched acceptance set and enough examples per critical food/component slice; scale by coverage and error risk rather than image count alone.

consent_and_privacy_fields: Explicit opt-in for collection, annotation, model training, internal evaluation, commercial product improvement, and optional remote processing as separate purposes.
Country/market jurisdiction, processing region, retention version, deletion/withdrawal status, and whether the participant permits derived masks/embeddings to remain after raw-photo deletion.
No faces or unrelated people where possible; strip EXIF/GPS, filenames, device identifiers, and free-text personal data before annotation/storage.
Participant/household/meal/recipe/device IDs must be opaque and separable from account identity; support deletion and export of source photos, labels, and derived artifacts.
capture_protocol: Capture ordinary phone RGB images in overhead and oblique views, with an optional guided short multi-view sequence; record device model, OS, camera mode, lighting, distance, and whether depth is available.

Record meal context: cuisine/region, dish/recipe name, brand where relevant, raw/cooked/served state, visible component list, hidden or mixed components, oils/sauces, edible versus inedible parts, and confidence of the human recorder.
Weigh empty container/tare, each component before plating when possible, the plated total, and leftovers if intake/consumed mass is a goal; store scale model, calibration check, timestamp, and units.
Use a repeatable reference object or calibrated depth/scale protocol only when it is acceptable for the user experience; record whether a reference was present in the image.
annotation_protocol: Annotate visible food versus non-food first, then semantic component masks, then separate repeated instances; use COCO polygons/RLE and a panoptic map only when thing/stuff definitions are explicit.
Attach a hierarchical taxonomy: canonical catalog item, visible component name, ingredient/recipe constituent, raw/cooked state, and an explicit visible/hidden/uncertain/occluded status.
Require two independent annotators for critical masks and ingredient labels, with adjudication for disagreement; store inter-annotator IoU/agreement and an uncertainty reason.

Validate mask geometry, class IDs, no invalid overlaps, image/mask dimensions, component-count consistency, and whether per-component weights sum to the independently measured total within a documented tolerance.
split_policy: Split by participant/household, recipe or meal instance, device, venue, and capture date where feasible; keep all frames/views/incremental weights for one meal in one split.
Hold out a culturally and geographically diverse acceptance set, not only a random image split; publish slice counts and confidence intervals.
Keep a private production-like test set with unseen devices, lighting, cuisines, mixed dishes, small ingredients, sauces, and occlusions.
quality_gates: Image quality and privacy review before annotation; calibrated-scale checks; duplicate/near-duplicate detection; EXIF and identity scrub verification.
Coverage floors for critical classes and failure modes; mask inter-annotator agreement; label-audit samples; grams-sum and recipe-consistency checks.
Report item recall, class/mask metrics, grams MAE/bias/p90/within +/-20%, abstention risk, correction time, and device resource metrics by slice.

recommendation_for_supernutrition.executive_recommendation: Build a visible-component, local-first candidate pipeline and a separate weighed-portion evaluation program. Use permissively cleared sources for development, use FoodInsSeg/FoodSAM/UECFoodPixComplete for academic benchmarking or annotation design only where their terms allow, and do not claim exact grams or hidden-ingredient completeness from a single RGB photo.

ranked_shortlist.use: Mass/portion ground-truth design, regression-head pretraining, and depth/volume hypothesis testing.
ranked_shortlist.why: Only source in this set with per-ingredient grams and high-quality capture metadata; official README states CC BY 4.0 commercial permission.
ranked_shortlist.blocker: California cafeteria bias, no per-ingredient 2D masks, 181.4 GB archive, and archived repository.

ranked_shortlist.use: Wild phone-photo visible-food detection/instance segmentation benchmark and server baseline.
ranked_shortlist.why: Largest realistic public polygon corpus in this landscape with 24,119 images and 273 classes, plus MIT Detectron2/MMDetection starter code.
ranked_shortlist.blocker: Commercial/data rights and per-component mass ground truth require written confirmation; class/cuisine coverage is not global.

ranked_shortlist.use: Ingredient-instance mask research, label ontology design, and evaluation of repeated/occluded components.
ranked_shortlist.why: 119,048 ingredient-level instance masks and very dense multi-component images.
ranked_shortlist.blocker: Academic-only/non-commercial CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; use only as a research benchmark or obtain a separate license.

ranked_shortlist.use: Semantic segmentation baselines, cross-domain comparison, and teacher/annotation-tool experiments.
ranked_shortlist.why: Large pixel-mask datasets with complementary ingredient/cuisine distributions and established mIoU baselines.
ranked_shortlist.blocker: No instance IDs or grams; UEC is non-commercial research-only and FoodSeg103 data terms are not sufficiently explicit for a default commercial assumption.

ranked_shortlist.use: Guided multi-view capture and temporal mask stability acceptance tests.
ranked_shortlist.why: 25,284 annotated frames and explicit continuity/flicker/IoU-drift evaluation address a major gap in still-image benchmarks.
ranked_shortlist.blocker: Very recent, multi-source, heavy research setup with no clear public commercial license or unified ingredient taxonomy.

ranked_shortlist.why: Blender scenes provide masks cheaply and the paper demonstrates real-world transfer after fine-tuning.
ranked_shortlist.blocker: Sim-to-real gap and unclear asset/data license; cannot replace real consented phone photos.

staged_plan.deliverable: A reproducible server benchmark comparing a compact semantic model, a compact instance model, FoodSAM, and a multi-label candidate model on cleared public data plus 300-500 consented weighed meals.
staged_plan.exit_metrics: Per-class visible-component recall, missed-component rate, mask mIoU/mAP/mAR, top-k ingredient recall, calibration/abstention, and initial device latency/RAM measurements.

staged_plan.deliverable: Select one local detector/segmenter and one per-instance candidate/embedding head; freeze a versioned label ontology with visible/hidden/uncertain states and model/checkpoint hashes.
staged_plan.exit_metrics: Changed-slice metrics meet agreed floors, no critical class/cuisine/device regression, and physical Android/iOS benchmark records latency, memory, thermal, battery, and offline behavior.

staged_plan.deliverable: Add the weighed corpus and optional depth/scale/reference features as a separate portion adapter; keep nutrient numbers catalog-derived after user confirmation.
staged_plan.exit_metrics: Grams MAE/bias/p90 and within +/-20% on a private acceptance set, with explicit abstention and user-correction behavior for mixed dishes, sauces, occlusion, and unseen cuisines.

staged_plan.deliverable: Local-first visible-component suggestions, reversible user corrections, explicit uncertainty, and a consented remote fallback only for configured low-confidence/complex cases.
staged_plan.exit_metrics: No silent upload, no exact-gram or hidden-ingredient claim, signed model/config provenance, raw-photo deletion evidence, and post-launch monitoring by slice.

recommendation_for_supernutrition.architecture_alignment: Keep the model output as identification evidence and masks/assumptions, not nutrition truth. Map accepted candidates to the versioned catalog and serving calculation only after user confirmation; keep local and remote inference adapters independent and make photo transfer explicit and reversible.
